# Compacted Summary: Chapters 1–2 (Complete and Final – Updated 52)

## Setting and Time
- **Period**: Spring through late August of first year; Christmas/New Year period; now nearly three weeks into new year (1832) just after Lords threw out Reform Bill; now summer of first year; narrative extends into future years of Fred and Mary's marriage
- **Primary Locations**: Middlemarch, Lowick, Grange, Freshitt, Mirecombe, Salwick, Quenwick, Fenmere, Bryngate, Chalky Flats, Gulton, Highbury, Cheltenham, Tipton, Yoddrell's farm, Frick, Miremere, Riverston, Quallingham, Halsell Wood, Loamford, Brassing, Stone Court, Coldcombe, St. Peter's Place, Lowick Gate, Shrubs, Dunholt, Yorkshire, Staveton, Bilkley, Harrowgate, Melspring, Wilhaven, Salford

## Main Characters

**Dorothea**
- Recently widowed; residing at Lowick Manor
- **Financial Status**: Seven hundred a-year personal fortune; nineteen hundred a-year from Casaubon; three to four thousand ready money in bank; dislikes Casaubon's property
- **Conviction About Lydgate**: Feels convinced Lydgate's conduct not guilty
- **Plan to Help Lydgate**: Wrote brief note with check for thousand pounds
- **Discovery at Lydgate's House**: Saw Will seated with Rosamond close by, flushed and tearful, Will clasping her hands with low-toned fervor; laid down letter and left quickly
- **Night of Anguish**: Waves of suffering shaking her thoroughly; cried in loud whispers between sobs; lay on bare floor as night grew cold; saw two images—Rosamond and Will—tearing her heart
- **Morning Awakening**: Awoke with clearest consciousness of looking into eyes of sorrow; wrapped warm things around her; seated in great chair; soul liberated from terrible conflict; could sit with grief as lasting companion
- **Second Visit to Lydgate's House**: Spoke about injustice shown Lydgate; spoke quite simply, gathering firmness; experienced emotional breaking point; clasped Rosamond as if in shipwreck; experienced revulsion of feeling too strong to be called joy; immediate consciousness one of immense sympathy without check
- **Revelation from Rosamond**: Rosamond disclosed Will loves another woman (Dorothea); said Will claims no other woman existed beside Dorothea; said blame entirely hers; said he cannot reproach her anymore
- **Evening Encounter with Will in Library**: Could not receive him where husband's prohibition seemed to dwell; when door opened, did not move; he came towards her with doubt and timidity; Dorothea afraid of her own emotion; stood motionless, hindering her from unclasping her hands
- **Will's Explanation**: Affair now matter of gossip; idea of getting Bulstrode to apply money to public purpose brought him back; Bulstrode privately offered compensation for old injury and good income; told her if it were new hardship, new reason to cling to her; nothing could have changed him but thinking she was different, not so good as believed; said she would believe him better than he is except in one thing—his truth to her
- **Storm Scene and Hand-Clasping**: Stood silent with Will looking at evergreens tossed showing pale underside against blackening sky; lightning made them start and smile; when vivid flash lit each for other, Dorothea darted instantaneously from window; Will seized her hand with spasmodic movement; they stood with hands clasped like two children; turned faces towards each other with memory of his last words in them
- **Will's Despairing Words**: Said there is no hope for him; even if she loved him as well as he loves her, he shall most likely always be very poor; on sober calculation, creeping lot only certain; impossible they ever belong to each other; perhaps base of him to have asked for word; meant to go away into silence but has not been able
- **Will's Continued Bitterness**: Said it is cruel of her to speak that way; she may see beyond misery but he doesn't; it is unkind—throwing back his love as if trifle; they can never be married; mere toss up whether he shall ever do more than keep himself decently unless sells himself as pen and mouthpiece; could not offer himself to any woman, even if she had no luxuries to renounce
- **Heart Full of Words**: Her heart full of something she wanted to say but words too difficult; wholly possessed by them; debate was mute within her; very hard she could not say what she wanted
- **Will's Departure and Her Response**: Will looked out of window angrily; at last turned and stretched hand automatically towards hat, said with exasperation "Good-by"; in instant she spoke; Will had arms round her but she drew head back and held his away gently while speaking; large tear-filled eyes looking at his very simply; spoke in sobbing childlike way: "We could live quite well on my own fortune—it is too much—seven hundred a-year—I want so little—no new clothes—and I will learn what everything costs"
- **Engagement and Plans**: Sent for uncle Mr. Brooke to Lowick; matter came about quite suddenly—neither had any idea two days ago; quite determined to act as she likes; Mr. Brooke will give her away but plans to cut off entail (will cost money and be troublesome)
- **Celia's Visit to Lowick**: Celia traveled to Lowick to influence Dorothea's mind; through girlhood felt she could act on her by word judiciously placed; as matron felt more able to advise childless sister; expressed shock at decision; said she has disappointed them all; said very bad; questioned how can marry Ladislaw with no estate; noted it shocks James dreadfully; called it all so different from what Dorothea has always been; referenced former reasons for marrying Casaubon (great soul, learning, age, dismalness) and expressed bewilderment at marrying Ladislaw instead

**Will Ladislaw**
- Passionate love for Dorothea
- **Public Scandal**: Genealogy now public knowledge via Bambridge's disclosure; described as having "queer genealogy"—high-spirited young lady, musical Polish patriot, with "grafting of the Jew pawnbroker"
- **Scene at Lydgate's House**: Seated with Rosamond on sofa, clasping both her upraised hands, speaking with low-toned fervor; when Rosamond became aware of Dorothea and snatched away her hands, Will looked round; meeting Dorothea's eyes with new lightning in them, seemed changing to marble
- **Anguish After Dorothea's Departure**: Stood motionless with Rosamond; looked towards spot where Dorothea stood; said sharply "Don't touch me!" with utterance like cut of lash; darted from Rosamond; wheeled round to other side of room with tips of fingers in pockets and head thrown back, looking fiercely; expressed inability to explain passion and that no other woman existed beside Dorothea
- **Plans to Return to Middlemarch**: As exile, had placed no stronger obstacle to return than own resolve—not iron barrier but state of mind liable to melt; as months went on, seemed more difficult to say why should not run down merely to hear something about Dorothea; hunger had tamed him and became very hungry for vision of certain form and sound of certain voice; took Riverston coach and came back again; made up mind he must go to Lydgate's that evening
- **Visit to Lydgate's House**: Received by Rosamond with languid coldness; Rosamond sat in silence bending over work; when poured tea, placed tiny bit of folded paper in his saucer; he secured it quickly; opened and read it by bed-candle; effect made cheeks and ears burn thinking of what occurred between Dorothea and Rosamond; felt uncertainty how far Dorothea might still feel dignity wounded; feared lasting flaw in her mind
- **Evening in Library with Dorothea**: Came towards her with more doubt and timidity than she had ever seen, afraid lest some look or word condemn him to new distance; took her hand and raised it to his lips with something like a sob; stood with hat and gloves in other hand; difficult to loose hand; felt very happy leaning on chair, not much afraid of anything she might feel; stood silent not looking at each other but at evergreens tossed showing pale underside of leaves; lightning made them start and smile; when vivid flash lit each for other, seized her hand with spasmodic movement; they stood with hands clasped like two children; turned faces towards each other; did not loose each other's hands
- **Expressions of Despair**: Said must be that they can never be married; it is cruel of her to speak that way—as if there were any comfort; it is unkind—throwing back his love as if trifle; expressed mere toss up whether shall ever do more than keep himself decently unless sells himself as pen and mouthpiece; could not offer himself to any woman, even if she had no luxuries to renounce; looked out of window angrily; at last turned, still resting against chair, and stretching hand automatically towards hat, said with exasperation, "Good-by"
- **Reversal When Dorothea Speaks**: When she spoke in sobbing childlike way about living well on her own fortune of seven hundred a-year, wanting so little, no new clothes, willing to learn what everything costs, Will had arms round her
- **Engagement**: Now engaged to marry Dorothea; has "objectionable position" and "bad origin" per Sir James

**Lydgate**: Has made final resolution to leave Middlemarch; declines continuing at Hospital; Dorothea sent him letter with check for thousand pounds; Rosamond made no reply when he mentioned Ladislaw sat with him; has accepted his narrowed lot with sad resignation; chosen fragile Rosamond and taken burden of her life upon his arms; full of timid care for his wife

**Rosamond Lydgate**: Married to Lydgate; disclosed to Dorothea that Will loves another woman (Dorothea), told her she has told Will and he cannot reproach her anymore; pride broken down between the two women; meek enough to nestle under old despised shelter; her husband had accepted his narrowed lot with sad resignation; has sent her daughters away to board at school on coast that crisis might be hidden from them

**Mary Garth**
- **Feelings for Fred**: Mind quite settled regarding marriage to Fred; said "Not a sad while, father—I mean to be merry"; expressed willingness and contentment; told father: "I shall be constant to Fred as long as he is constant to me. I don't think either of us could spare the other, or like any one else better, however much we might admire them"
- **Future Marriage and Life**: Will marry Fred Garth; achieves solid mutual happiness with him; becomes matronly, solid in figure like her mother; unlike her mother, gives boys little formal teaching, so Mrs. Garth alarmed lest they never well grounded in grammar and geography; nevertheless children found quite forward when went to school, perhaps because they liked nothing so well as being with their mother; brings forth three sons only, not discontented; Fred grateful to her for steadying influence; when Fred wished to have girl like her, she said laughingly "that would be too great a trial to your mother"; youngest boy very much what her father must have been when wore round jacket, showed marvellous nicety of aim in marbles and throwing stones for pears

**Fred Garth**
- **Present Situation**: Caleb Garth plans to tell Fred about Stone Court opportunity; Caleb will "come by-and-by"
- **Future Success**: Makes no failure but achieves solid mutual happiness with Mary; becomes rather distinguished in his side of county as theoretic and practical farmer; produces work on "Cultivation of Green Crops and the Economy of Cattle-Feeding" which won high congratulations at agricultural meetings; in Middlemarch admiration more reserved—most inclined to believe merit due to Mary since never expected Fred Vincy to write on turnips and mangel-wurzel; remains unswervingly steady some years after marriage; told Mary happiness half owing to Farebrother who gave him strong pull-up at right moment; never again wholly free from misled hopefulness—yield of crops or profits usually fell below estimate; always prone to believe could make money by horse purchase which turned out badly; Mary observed this fault of horse, not Fred's judgment; kept love of horsemanship but rarely allowed himself day's hunting; when did hunt, remarkable he submitted to be laughed at for cowardliness at fences, seeming to see Mary and boys sitting on five-barred gate or showing curly heads between hedge and ditch; gradually saved enough to become owner of stock and furniture at Stone Court; work Garth put into his hands carried him through "bad times" always present with farmers; had pleasant vision on winter evenings of bright hearth in wainscoted parlor, sorry for other men who could not have Mary for wife, especially Mr. Farebrother; told Mary magnanimously "He was ten times worthier of you than I was"; Mary answered "To be sure he was, and for that reason he could do better without me. But you—I shudder to think what you would have been—a curate in debt for horse-hire and cambric pocket-handkerchiefs!"
- **Children**: Has three boys; no daughters

**Caleb Garth**: Has tender concern for Mary's contentment; wants to ensure her mind quite settled; expresses belief woman must not force her heart—she'll do man no good by that; plans to tell Mary about Fred's Stone Court opportunity before telling Fred; Caleb's voice shook just perceptibly when speaking of Fred and Mary's marriage

## Family Reactions to Engagement

**Sir James Chettam**: Still in white indignation; said if Ladislaw had spark of honor would have gone out of country at once; said not surprised, day after Casaubon's funeral said what ought to be done but not listened to; unable to repress retort; called it perfectly scandalous; emphasized delicacy ought to have forbidden her seeing him again; listed grievances: Ladislaw takes her from proper rank into poverty, has meanness to accept such sacrifice, always had objectionable position, bad origin, man of little principle and light character; said cannot take Ladislaw into family and must speak for himself; acknowledged to himself (though ashamed) part of opposition stems from jealous repugnance not entirely different from his reaction to Casaubon; acknowledges marriage fatal for Dorothea; also motivated by undeniable fact that union of two estates—Tipton and Freshitt—was prospect that flattered him for his son and heir; when Mr. Brooke mentioned cutting off entail, Sir James felt sudden embarrassment, stoppage in throat, blushed

**Mr. Brooke** (Dorothea's uncle): Tried to dissuade her, pointed out poverty and abandoning position; spoke strongly to her but she quite determined to act as she likes; came to Lowick after she sent for him; it came about quite suddenly—neither had any idea two days ago; he put it strongly to her, did his duty, but she can act as she likes; advised Sir James to talk to Dorothea herself; mentioned fact that she dislikes Casaubon's property; can cut off entail; will cost money and be troublesome

**Mr. Cadwallader** (Rector): Said should not condemn as wrong action in strict sense because men have such poor opinion of each other; said they apt to consider act wrong because unpleasant to them; like many men who take life easily, had knack of saying home truth occasionally to those virtuously out of temper; said should not make any fuss about it, if she likes to be poor that is her affair; said nobody would have said anything if she had married young fellow because he was rich; noted plenty of beneficed clergy poorer than they will be; referenced own case: had hardly thousand a-year, was lout, nobody could see anything in him; said must take Ladislaw's part until hearing more harm of him

**Mrs. Cadwallader**: Said "there is usually a silent exception in such cases"; said only wonder to her is that any of them surprised; blamed them for doing nothing to hinder it; blamed Mr. Casaubon for preparing it all beautifully by making himself disagreeable

**Celia Chettam**: Said to Dorothea it is very bad, you have disappointed us all so; expressed disbelief that marriage "ever will be"; referenced all her plans; noted James would have taken any trouble for her; expressed shock at marrying Ladislaw with no estate

## Bulstrode Family Matters

**Mr. Bulstrode**: Has told his wife (Harriet) he intends not to sell land in neighborhood, but to leave it to her as safe provision; discussed making amends to Rosamond and her husband; mentioned Garth once thought of undertaking management of Stone Court; stock to remain as is, they to pay certain share of profits instead of ordinary rent; suggested this desirable beginning for young man in conjunction with employment under Garth; told Harriet she must make proposal to Garth herself; can put into her hands paper which Garth himself drew up, stating conditions; she can propose his renewed acceptance of them

**Harriet Bulstrode** (Mrs. Bulstrode): Expressed wish to do something for her brother's family (Fred and Mary Garth); thinks they are bound to make amends to Rosamond and her husband; mentioned Walter (presumably her brother) says Mr. Lydgate must leave town; seemed cut severely by Mrs. Casaubon's check; tears fell one after other, chin trembling; Bulstrode ached at sight of that grief-worn face, which two months before had been bright and blooming; aged to keep sad company with his own withered features

## Rumors and Unverified Claims
- Wife of Ridan Corrett confided to Ilzek Wexwood that bridge toll at Salwick skimmed every month
- Gossip from Pebin Wexwood claimed Thidrek Corrett and Rira Stenworth had been wed in secret
- Cotho Hollwood quit Wilhaven for good after a quarrel and took lodgings in Coldcombe
- Earlier rumors preserved: Lindson blood debt to Hollmere; Lindson mill ledger rewritten after flood; Salford granary fire set on purpose; old abbey at Salford second cellar; Bryngate pastures deed forged; silver chest buried beneath Mirecombe well; Quenwick chapel vault opens only for living person with jade ring and oak comb; Dunholt toll bridge belonged to Wexwood family

## Minor Characters and Incidental Details
- Ben and Letty Garth: Uncle and aunt before well in their teens; disputed whether nephews or nieces more desirable; Ben contended girls good for less than boys, shown by petticoats; Letty argued from books that God made coats of skins alike for both Adam and Eve, noted East men too wore petticoats; Ben answered "The more spooneys they!"; appealed to Mrs. Garth whether boys better than girls; Mrs. Garth pronounced both alike naughty but boys undoubtedly stronger, could run faster, throw with more precision to greater distance; Ben well satisfied; Letty took it ill, superiority stronger than her muscles
- Various townspeople in atmospheric fragments: Pebin Wexwood, Mazek (various), Ulvie Hollwood, Aessa Hollwood, Ellan, Jolia Hollett, Thidrek Corrett, Halan Hollett; remarks about weather, harvest, lame horse, salt prices, rain; baker's boy late, line at oven grew long; rain threatened but held off
